ch13.note: In Chinese custom red is the color of joy and celebration, white and black the colors of mourning. To bring a condolence gift in a red envelope treats the death as a 'happy funeral' (喜丧)—the fitting, even auspicious, end of someone who has died old and full of years—rather than an occasion for grief.

ch13.anchor: not a man of Fujian or Guangdong
ch13.note: The overwhelming majority of overseas Chinese came from the two southern coastal provinces of Fujian and Guangdong, and their communities abroad were knit by shared native place and dialect. For a man from Jiangsu, to the north, to win standing among them was therefore genuinely out of the ordinary.

China's staple divides along the Yangtze: the wheat-eating north lives on noodles, dumplings, and steamed bread, the south on rice. The two northern agents' craving for 'wheaten fare' in the rice-eating south is thus a matter of regional identity, not mere appetite.
Nguyễn is by far the commonest Vietnamese surname, borne by a large fraction of the whole people—which is why, a little later, a cousin's sharing it passes as unremarkable.

ch13.anchor: a scholar who had failed of the examinations
ch13.note: For over a thousand years the road to office and gentry standing ran through the imperial civil-service examinations. Candidates climbed a ladder of degrees—the licentiate (秀才) won at the local level, the 'provincial graduate' (举人) above it, and the metropolitan jinshi at the top—so 'failing the examinations,' 'placing first,' and stipends tied to a degree all measure a man's exact rank in that system. It was abolished in 1905.

The standard honorific for Sun Yat-sen (孙中山 / 孙逸仙, 1866–1925), founder of the revolutionary Tongmenghui and, in 1912, of the Republic of China, whose first provisional president he became. Revered by the Nationalists as the movement's founding sage; both Chiang and, in his fashion, Wang claimed his mantle.

The image pin ji si chen (牝鸡司晨), 'the hen that heralds the dawn,' from the Book of Documents: for a woman to seize the authority proper to a man was held an omen of ruin for a house or a state. Chen levels it at Chen Bijun's mastery over her husband, Wang Jingwei.

ch13.anchor: served Qin in the morning and Chu at night
ch13.note: The idiom zhao Qin mu Chu (朝秦暮楚): in the Warring States, small powers caught between the great rivals Qin and Chu would side now with one, now with the other—hence fickle, self-serving allegiance that keeps to no side.

Traditional Chinese years are named in a repeating sixty-year cycle formed by pairing ten 'heavenly stems' with twelve 'earthly branches.' Gengxu is one such name, here 1910; the famous xinhai year of the 1911 Revolution is the next but one in the same cycle.

This and the other verse titles in these pages—'The Beautiful Lady Yu,' 'The River All Red,' and the rest—are names of fixed ci tune-patterns: each names a set metrical and tonal template that a poet fills with new words. The title identifies the form, not the subject, so two poems bearing the same title need have nothing in common in content.
